8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":17,"verseId":6,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Action and Fruit","totalVerses":33,"verseData":{"id":"v17_6","number":6,"title":"The Central Dilemma: Permanent Action or Lost Cause?","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"If until the time of ripening Action had to remain in place, it would have to be permanent. If it has ceased, then having ceased, How will a fruit arise?"},"philosophy":{"insight":"The chapter's PIVOTAL verse — the permanence/annihilation dilemma of karmic continuity: (1) If action persists until its fruit ripens → permanent (contradicts impermanence). (2) If action ceases → how does a ceased cause produce a later effect? This dilemma underlies every theory of karma and haunts all non-Mādhyamika schools.","madhyamaka":"The dilemma: karma either nityam (permanent — remaining until ripening) or niruddham (ceased — vanished). If permanent: contradicts Buddhist impermanence. If ceased: violates causality (no cause → no effect). Every school must answer: how does a past, ceased action produce a future result? This is the karma problem.","quantum":"Wave function evolution: quantum information persists through wave function evolution without the system being \"permanent\" or \"annihilated.\" The wave function isn't a fixed thing (not permanent) but carries information forward (not lost). This is the quantum solution to persistence without permanence.","bridge":"Both karma and QM face the persistence problem: how does something persist without being permanent? QM: wave function evolution (neither fixed nor lost). Buddhism: dependent arising (neither permanent nor annihilated). Both resolve the dilemma by rejecting the binary.","accessible":"If you throw a ball and it has to stay in your hand until it's caught (permanent), that's absurd. But if the ball vanishes after you throw it (ceased), how does it ever arrive? Something must carry the \"action\" forward without being permanent. That's the puzzle.","twoTruths":"The dilemma arises from assuming inherent existence (ultimate level). Conventionally, actions cease and later produce results through dependent arising — no permanence or annihilation needed. The dilemma dissolves when inherent existence is abandoned.","commonMisconception":"NOT an unsolvable problem. The dilemma only arises IF you assume inherent existence. Dependent arising (conventional, empty) resolves it: actions cease conventionally but their causal influence persists through the empty continuum."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Wave Function Evolution — Persistence Without Permanence","score":72,"strength":"High","explanation":"Wave functions persist (carry information forward) without being permanent (they evolve). Like karma: causal influence persists without the action being permanent. Both resolve the persistence dilemma.","caveat":"Wave function evolution is a mathematical formalism. Karmic continuity is a metaphysical/ethical principle. The parallel is about persistence without permanence."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"A dilemma fork: left path = \"Action stays\" (freezes into permanent block), right path = \"Action ceases\" (vanishes into nothing, no fruit appears). Both paths fail. A middle path (dependent arising) shows action ceasing while its influence flows forward.","educationalGoal":"User sees the central dilemma of karmic theory: permanence vs. annihilation. Both extremes fail. The middle way (dependent arising) is needed."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Why is this the chapter's pivotal verse?","a":"Because it identifies the FUNDAMENTAL PROBLEM that every theory of karma must solve. VV.1-5 described karma. V.6 asks: HOW does it work? Every subsequent verse in the chapter is a response to this question.","realLifeExample":"A detective story where v.6 is the crime scene. Everything before (vv.1-5) is the setup; everything after (vv.7-33) is the investigation."},{"q":"Why would remaining action be permanent?","a":"If an action must persist UNCHANGED until its result appears, it exists without changing from the moment of action to the moment of fruition. Existing without change = permanent. But all conditioned things are impermanent — so permanent action contradicts Buddhist metaphysics.","realLifeExample":"If a letter had to remain in your hand until the recipient reads it, you'd be permanently holding letters. The postal system solves this: the letter leaves your hand but still reaches the recipient through an intermediary system."},{"q":"Why is a ceased action problematic?","a":"If the action COMPLETELY ceases — utterly vanishes — what connects it to the later result? Ex nihilo nihil fit (nothing comes from nothing). A completely non-existent cause can't produce an effect. The cause-effect link seems to require the cause's continued existence.","realLifeExample":"If you delete a computer program, it can't run later. Something must persist (the file, a backup) for the program to function. Complete deletion = no later execution."},{"q":"How do different schools try to solve this?","a":"Sarvāstivāda: all dharmas exist in past, present, and future (avoids cessation but risks eternalism). Sautrāntika: seeds/continuum (vv.7-8). Yogācāra: store-consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna). Each proposes a mechanism for persistence without permanence. Nāgārjuna: emptiness resolves the dilemma.","realLifeExample":"Different email services solve message delivery differently (SMTP, IMAP, cloud storage). Each proposes a different mechanism for the same function: getting the message from sender to receiver."},{"q":"How does dependent arising solve the dilemma?","a":"Dependent arising rejects the binary: action is neither inherently permanent nor inherently ceased. It ceases CONVENTIONALLY while its causal influence continues through the dependent continuum. No inherent permanence (it ceases). No inherent annihilation (its influence continues).","realLifeExample":"A wave in the ocean: the individual water molecules don't travel with the wave (not permanent), but the wave's energy propagates through the medium (not annihilated). The wave ceases at each point but its influence continues forward."},{"q":"Why does this dilemma haunt ALL non-Mādhyamika schools?","a":"Because every school that posits inherent existence for actions must explain how that inherent existence persists or ceases. If it persists: permanence. If it ceases: annihilation. The dilemma is intrinsic to inherent existence. Only by abandoning inherent existence (Mādhyamika) does the dilemma dissolve.","deeper":"V.6 is arguably the most important verse in Ch.17. It identifies a problem that occupied Buddhist philosophy for centuries: the mechanism of karmic continuity. The Sarvāstivāda, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Mādhyamika schools each developed their central doctrines partly in response to this question. Nāgārjuna's solution (emptiness + dependent arising) is the simplest and most elegant: the problem only arises under inherent existence. Remove inherent existence, and the dilemma vanishes."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"What is the central dilemma of v.6?","options":["A) No dilemma","B) If action persists until fruition → permanent (contradicts impermanence).
